signal.topic_name: AI Agents Are Replacing Junior Developers

scenario.title: AI Just Fired Junior Devs. Here's the Receipts.
scenario.angle: Instead of fear-mongering, we flip the script: the junior devs who thrive will be the ones who learn to manage AI agents — making this a skill gap story, not a job loss story.

scenes.voiceover: Andrej Karpathy just said junior devs are being replaced. He's not wrong. But here's what nobody's telling you.
scenes.visual_description: Black screen. White bold text slams in word by word. Karpathy's face thumbnail flashes for 0.5s then cuts to blinking cursor on a terminal.

scenes.voiceover: Devin AI just completed a 2-week sprint in 45 minutes. Real ticket. Real codebase. No Stack Overflow.
scenes.visual_description: Split screen: left shows Devin AI's interface auto-writing code, right shows a Jira ticket timer melting from 14 days to 45 minutes.

scenes.voiceover: But wait — someone has to tell Devin what to build, catch its mistakes, and ship it. That's not a bot. That's you.
scenes.visual_description: Developer at desk looks alarmed, then slowly grins. Camera slowly zooms in on the moment the smile appears. Subtle glow effect on face.
scenes.caption_overlay: The job didn't disappear. It upgraded. 🔺

scenes.voiceover: The devs winning right now know prompt engineering, agent orchestration, and how to QA AI output. Three skills. Learn them.
scenes.visual_description: Three skills fly in one by one with neon color pops: PROMPT ENGINEERING, AGENT ORCHESTRATION, AI QA. Each word hits on a beat.

scenes.voiceover: One dev in Austin now manages 4 AI agents. His output? 10x a senior engineer. His salary? Up 40 percent.
scenes.visual_description: Fast cuts: laptop with multiple agent dashboards, Slack notifications flooding in with completed tasks, a pay stub blurred with an upward arrow.

scenes.voiceover: So yeah — junior devs ARE being replaced. The ones who don't adapt. Are you going to be one of them?
scenes.visual_description: Screen returns to the opening blinking cursor. Text types itself: 'Are you the dev... or the one being replaced?' Cursor blinks. Hard cut to black.
scenes.caption_overlay: ⚠️ Junior Devs Are Being Replaced — which side are you on?

hook_test.format_reference: Wait, what? — Hook with surprising claim → proof → bigger reveal
hook_test.viral_proof: This format mirrors the 'They're shutting down your career' cold-open style used by @techbro and @levelsio-style creators, consistently hitting 10M–40M views. Karpathy name-drop in second 1 triggers authority bias. The reframe in scene 3 is the classic 'BUT WAIT' pivot that drives shares and saves.
hook_test.why_it_works: Opens with a credible threatening claim (shock), immediately validates it with data (proof), then delivers an unexpected power-shift reframe (relief + hope). The emotional arc — fear → confirmation → empowerment — is the exact dopamine loop that drives completion rate above 80% and mass shares in career-anxious tech audiences.

verdict.message_analysis: The message is crystal clear and original: junior devs aren't being eliminated, they're being *upgraded* — those who master AI agent management will thrive. Every scene serves this thesis. Scene 1 sets up the fear (shock), Scene 2 validates it (proof), Scene 3 flips it (reframe), Scenes 4-5 deliver the solution (skill stack + proof of concept), and Scene 6 closes the loop with urgency. No filler. The angle cuts against fear-mongering and instead positions the viewer as the agent of their own survival — highly shareable because it's empowering, not panic-inducing.
verdict.scroll_stop_analysis: The hook is devastating. 'Andrej Karpathy just said junior devs are being replaced' + Karpathy thumbnail + cursor blink in 4 seconds hits all three dopamine triggers: authority (Karpathy), social proof (threat), and pattern interrupt (kinetic text + impact music). Scene 2 sustains with the 14-day → 45-minute visual (jaw-drop moment). Scene 3's reframe + slow zoom on the grin is the emotional pivot that converts scroll-stoppers into savers. Pacing is tight throughout. Pattern interrupts are consistent (2-4 per scene). The silence at the end (Scene 6) is gutsy and works—it forces the viewer to sit with the question. This would absolutely feel native on TikTok, not preachy.
